system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2177-08-13 05:27:00 to 2177-08-16 14:07:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, insulin-dependent diabetes, morbid obesity, and recent cellulitis was readmitted due to recurrent erythema, swelling, and fever in the left lower extremity just days after prior discharge. Imaging revealed subcutaneous gas suggestive of necrotizing fasciitis, prompting emergent surgical debridement. He underwent three procedures: initial debridement, a washout with wound vac placement, and a second debridement for progressive tissue involvement. Cultures were negative, likely due to prior antibiotics. He was managed with vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and clindamycin (later discontinued), along with insulin for glucose control. His infection resolved, white count normalized, and he transitioned to oral intake and ambulation. He was discharged to a rehabilitation facility on continued IV antibiotics with plans for follow-up in infectious disease and surgery clinics.
problems: Cellulitis and abscess of leg, except foot
Secondary diabetes mellitus with neurological manifestations, not stated as uncontrolled, or unspecified
Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Unspecified chronic liver disease without mention of alcohol

COMPARISON:  Chest radiographs from ___ and ___,
and outside hospital chest CT from ___.

FRONTAL AND LATERAL CHEST RADIOGRAPHS:  The lungs appear clear without
confluent opacity.  There is no pulmonary edema or pleural effusions.  No
pneumothorax is evident.  Cardiomediastinal widening corresponds with
mediastinal lipomatosis seen on concurrent CT.  A right PICC terminates in the
mid SVC.  

IMPRESSION:  No acute cardiopulmonary process.  Mediastinal lipomatosis.

INDICATION:  History of left anterior shin necrotizing fasciitis with recent
chest pain and concern for pulmonary embolism.  Please evaluate for DVT.

COMPARISON:  Left lower extremity ultrasound from ___.

FINDINGS:  This study is limited secondary to patient body habitus.  Grayscale
and color Doppler imaging of the left common femoral, superficial femoral, and
popliteal veins demonstrate normal compressibility, flow, and augmentation
throughout.  Normal flow and compressibility is seen within both left
posterior tibial veins.  The left peroneal veins were not well imaged, similar
to the prior study from ___.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of left lower extremity DVT.  Limited evaluation of
left peroneal veins.

INDICATION:  Acute onset shortness of breath, hypoxemia, tachycardia, seen at
outside hospital ED last night where a suboptimal CTA of the chest was
performed (indeterminate for pulmonary embolism).  The patient was heparinized
empirically and transferred here for repeat imaging.  Please evaluate for
pulmonary embolism.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axial images were acquired through the chest without the
administration of intravenous contrast material.  Subsequently, rapid axial
images were acquired through the chest during infusion of 100 cc of
intravenous Omnipaque contrast material.  Multiplanar reformats were
performed, including maximum intensity projection oblique reformats.  The
total DLP is 1006 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  Chest CT from ___ dated ___.

FINDINGS:  There are nonocclusive filling defects within segmental branches of
the left lower lobe pulmonary arteries (3:39), consistent with emboli.  There
is no leftward bowing of the interventricular septum to suggest right heart
strain or reflux of contrast into the IVC.  Extensive mediastinal lipomatosis
is again seen.  There is no mediastinal, hilar, or axillary lymphadenopathy.

There is minimal bilateral dependent atelectasis in both lower lobes.  There
is no focal consolidation.  The airways are patent to the subsegmental levels
bilaterally.  A right PICC ends in the mid SVC.

BONE WINDOW:  No suspicious lytic or blastic lesions are identified. 
Multilevel degenerative changes of the thoracic spine are noted.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Scattered nonocclusive emboli in left lower lobe segmental arteries,
without evidence of right heart strain or pulmonary infarction.

2.  Unchanged mediastinal lipomatosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were brought in last night after having shortness of breath and chest pain while showering. Can you tell me how you're feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m feeling better now. The chest pain and shortness of breath are gone, but I was really scared last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You were given heparin at the other hospital because they suspected a blood clot in your lungs, called a pulmonary embolism. The scan they did wasn’t clear, so we’re repeating tests here to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So I might have a clot in my lungs? But I feel fine now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s possible. Sometimes symptoms come on suddenly and then improve, but the clot can still be there. We’ll do a better CT scan today to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And what about my leg wound? It’s still got the vacuum dressing on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The surgical team saw you this morning. They checked the wound on your left leg and changed the dressing. It looks clean, no signs of infection right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried about it getting worse again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too, especially after your recent surgery for necrotizing fasciitis. But right now, our main concern is ruling out or confirming the pulmonary embolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What happens if the scan shows a clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it does, you’ll stay on heparin through your IV, and we’ll start a blood thinner called warfarin. You’ll need to take that for several months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It depends on the results. If we confirm the clot, you’ll stay a few days so we can monitor your blood levels and make sure the warfarin is working safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my diabetes—am I still on my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on your usual glargine and sliding scale with NovoLOG. We’re monitoring your sugars closely. They’ve been a bit high but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want them spiking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. We got the ultrasound of your leg to check for a clot there. It’s negative—no deep vein thrombosis. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the clot isn’t in my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in the major veins we could see. The small veins were hard to image because of your body habitus, but we don’t think there’s a significant clot there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the chest scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling it for this afternoon. Once we have the results, we’ll know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I have the results of your chest CT. It shows small blood clots in the arteries of your left lung. They’re not blocking the flow completely, and your heart looks okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So I do have a pulmonary embolism?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s not severe. No lung damage or strain on your heart. That’s why you’re feeling okay now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did this happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Several factors: your recent immobility after surgery, obesity, and possibly your inflammatory conditions. These increase clotting risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on IV heparin for now. We started warfarin yesterday—5 mg daily. We’ll adjust the dose based on your INR blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long until the warfarin works?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It takes about 5 days. We’ll keep the heparin going until your INR is in the right range for two days in a row.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my leg wound—can I keep the vacuum dressing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the surgeons recommend continuing it. But when you go back to rehab, they may switch to a wet-to-dry dressing temporarily for transport.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that slow healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not significantly. You’ll go back to the vacuum dressing when you arrive. The wound is healing, just slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your INR came back at 1.8 today. It’s rising, but not quite in the target range yet. We’ve increased your warfarin to 7.5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? Higher dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s common. We monitor your blood daily to avoid bleeding risks. Your platelets and kidney function are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The urine test yesterday—was there an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the urine culture showed mixed bacteria, but it’s likely contamination. No treatment needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Your INR is now 2.5 and holding. That’s in the target range. If it stays there tomorrow, we can stop the heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll just be on the warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll need to take it every day for about six months. You’ll see a hematologist as an outpatient to manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Can I go back to my usual list?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your other medications are continuing—your insulin, blood pressure meds, arthritis drugs, and eye drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today to the rehab facility. Your pulmonary embolism is being treated, and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will I still need the IV heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. You’ll get it through your PICC line. The rehab team will continue it until your INR stays in range for 48 hours. Then they’ll stop it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking 7.5 mg daily. They’ll check your INR every day. You’ll follow up with surgery and hematology clinics soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my leg wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll switch to a wet-to-dry dressing for transport, then back to the vacuum dressing at rehab. Keep following the wound care instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay on top of your meds, watch for any bleeding or shortness of breath, and keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, morbid obesity, diabetes, and recent necrotizing fasciitis of the left lower extremity was admitted from an extended care facility after developing acute shortness of breath, chest pain, and hypoxia following a shower. He was transferred on empiric heparin for suspected pulmonary embolism after an indeterminate CT at an outside hospital. Upon arrival, he was stable and asymptomatic. A repeat CT angiogram confirmed scattered nonocclusive pulmonary emboli in the left lower lobe without right heart strain. He remained on intravenous heparin and was started on warfarin, which was titrated to 7.5 mg daily as his INR rose toward the therapeutic range. The surgical team evaluated his left leg wound with vacuum dressing and recommended continuation of wound care. He was discharged to the rehabilitation facility on continued IV heparin and warfarin with plans for hematologic and surgical follow-up.
